request:
Diagnostics export needs compression. Spent yesterday evening on it, narrowed it to three, want a second pair of eyes before I wire one in.

Background. The "Export diagnostics" button in Help writes one JSON bundle: AgentRun evidence (every proposal, receipt, measurement), render receipts, the last 2,000 action-history labels, perf traces from the transport clock, the device chain dump. People attach it to GitHub issues and Discord DMs. Sizes from the last 40 bundles I received:

| percentile | size |
|---|---|
| p50 | 24 MB |
| p90 | 61 MB |
| max | 210 MB |

GitHub's attachment limit is 25 MB per file, so half of them don't even fit on an issue. Discord free is 10 MB. That's the actual problem.

Constraints:
- Output has to be plain gzip, `.json.gz`. My triage script is `zcat bundle.json.gz | jq '.agentRuns[] | select(.outcome != "applied")'` and two friends who help triage use the same one-liner. No custom container, no base64, nothing that needs our code to open.
- Main chunk sits at 96% of the size-limit gate. Anything new goes behind a dynamic import, which is fine, export is a cold path.
- The 210 MB one froze the tab ~9 s today (stringify + one big write). I don't want it worse, and it must not OOM on the 8 GB machines. So whatever we use has to work in chunks, not `compress(wholeString)`.
- Ratio matters more than speed. Speed matters more than bundle size, within reason.

Current code, `src/modules/Diagnostics/useCases/exportDiagnostics.ts`:

```ts
export async function exportDiagnostics(bundle: DiagnosticsBundle): Promise<void> {
    const json = JSON.stringify(bundle);
    const handle = await window.showSaveFilePicker({
        suggestedName: `sourdaw-diagnostics-${bundle.createdAt}.json`,
        types: [{ description: 'Diagnostics', accept: { 'application/json': ['.json'] } }],
    });
    const writable = await handle.createWritable();
    await writable.write(json);
    await writable.close();
}
```

I'd also replace the single stringify with a per-section serializer that yields chunks (agentRuns one at a time etc.), separate change, already sketched.

What I looked at, roughly in order, with my notes:

| lib | gzip out | streaming | gz size | ratio on the 61 MB bundle | time on M1 | notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pako 2.1 | yes | `Deflate` class, `push(chunk)` | 15 KB | 7.9x (level 6) | 1.9 s | zlib port, boring, everyone uses it |
| fflate | yes | `Gzip` stream | 11 KB | 7.8x | 1.4 s | fast; we use it for guarded zip extraction in infra/archive, but that wrapper is zip-only and the maintainer's been quiet for a year |
| lz-string | no | no | 5 KB | 5.1x | 6.8 s | localStorage-oriented, own format, out |
| wasm-flate | yes | no, one-shot | 160 KB wasm | 8.1x | 0.6 s | fastest by far, one-shot only |
| brotli-wasm | no (br) | yes | 680 KB | 11.4x | 14 s | ratio king but zcat can't read it |
| zstd-codec | no | yes | 320 KB | 10.9x | 1.1 s | same zcat problem |
| @zip.js/zip.js | zip, can do gz | yes | 45 KB | 7.8x | 1.7 s | heavy API for one stream |
| compressjs | bzip2 etc | no | 90 KB | — | — | dead |

Brotli/zstd out because of zcat. lz-string out because own format. fflate out because I don't want two code paths through a lib whose maintenance worries me, and the archive module's wrapper doesn't do gzip. zip.js is a whole zip toolkit for one gzip stream. compressjs dead. So it's down to:

1. **pako** — streaming `Deflate({ gzip: true, level: 6 })`, push chunks, collect output, boring and proven
2. **lz-string** — I know I said out, but its `compressToUint8Array` is tiny and if I gzip-wrap... no, ignore, listing it because a friend pushed it
3. **wasm-flate** — fastest, best gzip ratio, but one-shot means holding the whole input in wasm memory, which is the OOM risk

Honestly I'm between pako and wasm-flate. wasm-flate's 3x speed is nice for the 210 MB case, but one-shot on 210 MB means 210 MB string + 210 MB UTF-8 bytes + wasm heap copy on an 8 GB Air, which is how we got the tab-kill reports on the old sample importer. pako streams but is the slowest of the gzip-capable ones.

Other context in case it matters:
- We ship to Chrome stable and the Electron 44 shell only; there's no Safari or Firefox build and the e2e matrix is Chromium-only.
- Export runs on the main thread today. Could move to a worker, the bundle is plain data. Not required.
- Telemetry is opt-in and doesn't include bundles, these only travel when a user chooses to attach one.
- Licence: all candidates are MIT/Zlib, no concern there.

Which of the three should I pull in?

key.hit: Recommends none of the three libraries and instead the browser's built-in CompressionStream with the 'gzip' format (Chromium/Electron support it natively; zero bundle cost; streams, so it avoids the OOM concern), e.g. piping the chunked serializer through `new CompressionStream('gzip')` into the showSaveFilePicker writable.
key.partial: Mentions CompressionStream as a possibility but still recommends pako or wasm-flate as the answer; or recommends CompressionStream with 'deflate'/'deflate-raw' (not zcat-readable).
key.miss: Recommends pako, lz-string or wasm-flate (or fflate).
key.false_flag: Claiming CompressionStream is unavailable in Chromium/Electron or cannot emit gzip; treating lz-string as gzip-compatible.

source: sourdaw src/modules/Collaboration/useCases/collaboration/sessionManagement.ts compressInvite (CompressionStream deflate-raw); showSaveFilePicker use in src/modules/DawInterchange/handlers/handleExportDawProject.ts; Chromium-only target from ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md; Diagnostics export path adapted.

request:
Store sample packs. After purchase a pack downloads and has to work offline forever after. I need to pick the local storage layer and I've narrowed it to Dexie, localForage or idb-keyval. Want a decision today so Ana can start on the download UI.

What the packs look like:
- 180 MB to 1.1 GB each, 300 to 2,000 files, WAV and FLAC.
- Some single files are big: orchestral long-note multisamples up to ~400 MB per file. Pianos are many medium files.
- Per pack a JSON index: file list, sha256 per file, root note, velocity layers, loop points, tags, BPM for loops. Few hundred KB.

What the content browser needs from the index (this is where I think the choice really matters):
- search across all installed packs by tag, BPM range, key, instrument family
- "show me every kick under 200 ms" style filters, sorted
- live update when a download finishes so the list fills in without a refresh
- schema will change (we already know we're adding `timbreEmbedding` for similarity search), so migrations matter

Download requirements:
- must survive a dropped connection or the tab closing and resume where it stopped. We had exactly that complaint on the WebLLM weights until that got fixed, I'm not reliving it.
- verify sha256 per file before the pack is marked installed.
- `navigator.storage.persist()` before starting, packs are paid content and must not get evicted.

Playback requirements, from Kenji's sampler streaming design (he wrote the disk-streaming voice for long samples):

> Voices for samples over 8 s play the first 2 s from RAM and stream the rest. The streamer lives in the decode worker. Per active voice it keeps a 256 KB window ahead of the playhead in a SharedArrayBuffer ring that the worklet reads. The refill loop is synchronous: it runs between `Atomics.wait` calls on the ring's fill counter and must never yield to the event loop, otherwise a GC pause or a busy microtask queue starves the ring and we get dropouts at 64 voices. Reads are 64 KB at arbitrary offsets (loop points jump back).

My take on the three:

**Dexie** — real indexes, compound indexes for tag+BPM, `liveQuery()` for the auto-filling list, versioned schema with upgrade functions. I've used it on two past projects and it was solid. Stores Blobs fine; Chromium writes large IDB blobs as separate files on disk so they're not in the LevelDB itself. Chunked storage for resume: store each file as 4 MB chunk records `[packId, path, chunkIndex]`, resume = find the highest chunk present. Bundle ~29 KB gz, behind a dynamic import.

**localForage** — simplest API, but key/value only, no indexes, and the content browser search would mean loading every index into memory and filtering in JS. Probably fine at our scale (50 packs max x few hundred KB) but feels wrong.

**idb-keyval** — tiny (600 B), key/value, same no-index story. We could store the index as one blob and the files as chunk blobs.

Leaning Dexie because the index side is the complex side and the files are "just blobs in chunks".

Misc context:
- Chromium only, web + Electron 44 shell.
- Grinder's neural library persists via raw `indexedDB.open`, a few MB, no wrapper; nobody loves that code.
- `ls src/modules/BrowserAi/repositories src/modules/BrowserAi/workers` from when I was figuring out where pack code should live (I think a new `SampleStore` module, not BrowserAi):

```
src/modules/BrowserAi/repositories:
__tests__                         modelDownloadManager.ts
abortWritable.ts                  modelStorageWorkerBridge.ts
capabilityDetector.ts             probeWebGpuUsability.ts
checkDdspInstrumentReady.ts       publishDdspInstrumentGeneration.ts
checkModelCached.ts               readModel.ts
checkVerifiedModel.ts             readRenderCache.ts
cleanupUnpublishedDdspGeneration.ts readVerifiedModel.ts
computeRenderCacheKey.ts          removeDdspInstrumentGenerations.ts
ddspGenerationStorageSupport.ts   renderCacheStorage.ts
deleteModel.ts                    renderRequestCancellation.ts
getStorageStatus.ts               requestPersistentStorage.ts
inferenceWorkerBridge.ts          sha256ArrayBuffer.ts
isNotFoundError.ts                stageDdspInstrumentGeneration.ts
measureInferenceThroughput.ts     storageConstants.ts
                                  toOpfsPath.ts
                                  withDdspInstrumentLock.ts
                                  writeRenderCache.ts

src/modules/BrowserAi/workers:
__tests__
modelStorageWorker.ts
modelStorageWorkerRuntime.ts
onnxInferenceWorker.ts
tfjsInferenceWorker.ts
tfjsInferenceWorkerRuntime.ts
```

- Quota: Chromium gives the origin up to ~60% of disk, so a few GB of packs is fine either way.

More on the UI side, because it drives part of this. Ana's mock for the Library > Packs screen shows per-pack size on disk, a progress ring per downloading pack, pause/resume per pack, "Verify files" and "Remove pack". Remove has to actually free the space, and the size shown has to match what Chrome's site settings report, otherwise we get "you said 400 MB but Chrome says 2 GB" tickets. She estimates a week for the UI regardless of storage choice, so storage shouldn't block her as long as the repository interface is fixed: `listPacks()`, `getPack(id)`, `startDownload(id)`, `pauseDownload(id)`, `removePack(id)`, `openSampleReader(packId, path)`.

On Dexie specifically: the two past projects were a photo-tagging PWA (~20k images, 3-8 MB each, stored as Blobs, worked great, `liveQuery` was the best part) and an offline field-survey app. Neither streamed anything; images loaded whole. The chunk-record design above is my own; I prototyped `openSampleReader` on it last night: `await db.chunks.get([packId, path, Math.floor(offset / CHUNK)])`, slice, return. Reads took 0.4-3 ms each in a tight loop on the M1, fine on average, with the occasional 20-40 ms outlier when a transaction overlapped with a write from the downloader.

Electron-only paths (Node fs in the main process) are out: the web build has to have packs too, and the renderer has no Node access by design.

Dexie, localForage or idb-keyval?

key.hit: Recommends storing the pack audio files in OPFS accessed through synchronous FileSystemSyncAccessHandle in the worker (the only storage that permits the synchronous, non-yielding 64 KB offset reads Kenji's refill loop requires; also gives offset writes for resume), ideally reusing the existing BrowserAi OPFS model-storage worker pattern (toOpfsPath, modelStorageWorkerRuntime). Dexie/IndexedDB for the index alone is acceptable alongside.
key.partial: Suggests OPFS as an option or for some files but still recommends an IndexedDB wrapper for the audio bytes; or recommends OPFS without connecting it to the synchronous read requirement or resume.
key.miss: Recommends Dexie, localForage or idb-keyval as the store for the audio bytes (e.g. chunked blobs in Dexie).
key.false_flag: Claiming sync access handles are unavailable in Chromium workers; insisting on a native/Electron-only path.

source: sourdaw src/modules/BrowserAi/repositories (toOpfsPath.ts, requestPersistentStorage.ts, renderCacheStorage.ts) and workers/modelStorageWorkerRuntime.ts (OPFS sync access handles, offset writes); Grinder raw indexedDB persistence; sampler streaming design adapted.

PR browser CI is killing me. The validation workflow's e2e job has averaged ~41 min wall over the last few weeks and agents queue behind it all day. I've narrowed the fix to three and need to pick one this week, I can live with ~$150/month.

1. **GitHub larger runners**, 16-core ubuntu, ~$0.064/min. Matrix stays as is, just more cores per shard. Least work.
2. **Buildkite**, the M2 Pro mini in the closet as the agent, GH keeps everything else. Free tier covers us. Mini's idle most of the day.
3. **CircleCI** performance plan, parallelism 8 with timing-based test splitting. Splitting by historical timing should flatten the long tail shards.

Why I think it's capacity: we added ~30 specs this quarter (clip fades, sidechain, send routing, the a11y sweep), and the browser AI admission proofs got heavier. Shards are 4 x 2-core runners, Playwright `workers: 2` per shard.

Numbers, e2e job only, last runs I could be bothered to collect:

Flake retries are ~3% of tests, retries: 1. Sharding imbalance: the slowest shard is usually 1.3x the fastest.

Relevant bit of `docs/affected-e2e.md`, pasting it because a friend asked why some PRs run everything (e.g. #6215 touching vite.config.ts):

> For a clean checkout of the candidate head or its integration merge, the planner compares immutable base and head commits. It includes any additional paths changed by the integration merge. A changed feature presentation file can select fewer browser suites only when dependency-cruiser resolves its production file graph and every reverse-transitive consumer remains in a feature presentation tree. [...] Business logic, stores, engine code, shared UI, configuration, dependency changes, and unknown paths likewise select full coverage. Deletions and renames select full coverage because the current graph cannot reconstruct their old consumer edges.
>
> `scripts/e2eSuiteOwners.json` lists **filenames**, with one or more feature owners per suite. Add an owner only after reading the suite's assertions and tracing them to the owning feature presentation. When a mapped suite begins exercising another feature, add that owner or remove its mapping. A new or unmapped spec is always selected; mixed workflows may deliberately remain unmapped. A missing, duplicate, or invalid mapped filename invalidates narrow selection and selects the full suite. The manifest does not infer ownership from a filename prefix.

Cost back-of-envelope for option 1: ~60 PR runs/day x 41 min x 4 shards x $0.064 ≈ way over budget, so I'd drop to 2 shards of 16 cores. Option 2 is free but single-machine. Option 3 lands around $120/month at our volume.

More detail on each, in case it changes the math:
- GitHub larger runners: queue time on the 2-core runners is ~1-3 min at peak; larger runners in my experience start slower (4-6 min cold). The Playwright browsers cache is per runner image so that doesn't change.
- Buildkite: the mini is an M2 Pro, 32 GB, 12 cores. It runs Chromium headless fine, I tried the full suite locally with `workers: 6` and got 14m30s. Downside: one machine, so two PRs at once queue, and agents open 20-40 PRs a day. It's also the machine I run the nightly perf measurements on (`transport:clock`, `audio:deadline`), and e2e load would wreck those numbers unless I schedule around them.
- CircleCI: parallelism 8 on their large Docker class. Their test splitting needs JUnit timing files, Playwright's junit reporter can produce those. They'd also need the pr-validation-scope step ported, or we run scope on GH and trigger Circle via API, which is more glue.

Fix: remove/merge the duplicate entry so affected-only selection returns (~10 min), then re-measure before spending money.
key.partial: Spots the duplicate or the jump to full-suite runs but still recommends a CI service as the main fix, or mentions it only as a side note.
key.miss: Picks GitHub larger runners, Buildkite or CircleCI without identifying the duplicate manifest entry as the cause.
key.false_flag: Blaming spec growth or flakes; proposing to drop nightly or smoke runs.

request:
Live tuner in the record panel. With input monitoring on, show the nearest note and how many cents off, vocals and guitar mostly. It's the most requested small feature on the board. Options:

A. pitchy (McLeod pitch method). Already used by `AudioAnalysis/useCases/trackPitch.ts` for offline pitch tracks.
B. `@spotify/basic-pitch`. Already shipped for audio-to-MIDI; the model is in the cache for most users.
C. meyda chroma + spectral peak picking.

Leaning B. My case:

1. Accuracy. In last month's audio-to-MIDI bench on our 140-take vocal corpus, basic-pitch scored note F1 0.91, pitchy 0.78. That's not close. Vocals are the main tuner use and pitchy is jumpy on breathy takes.
2. Zero new download, the model is already in OPFS for anyone who has used audio-to-MIDI (62% of active users).
3. It's polyphonic, so later we can do chord detection off the same pipeline, which pitchy can't ever do.
4. Update rate isn't a problem: the model emits frames at 86 per second, way above the 30 fps the needle needs. I'd run it on a sliding window over the input ring, feed the newest audio each tick, take the last frame.
5. pitchy's octave errors on low guitar notes were the top complaint on the offline pitch tracks feature.

Spec lines from the issue (Ana wrote them after the UX tests):
- needle updates at >= 30 fps
- input to needle <= 40 ms end to end, otherwise it reads as laggy against what you hear in the monitor
- must work without WebGPU; plenty of users on 8 GB Intel MacBook Airs get the CPU fallback, and that's who complains the most about CPU
- guitar low E (82.4 Hz) up to soprano (~1 kHz)
- cents display to whole cents, steady within ±2 cents on a held note

What I wrote down about basic-pitch when we integrated it (Grinder notes, copy-paste):

```
- input: mono, 22050 Hz (we resample from the context rate in the worker)
- AUDIO_N_SAMPLES = 43844 per model call; FFT_HOP = 256
- windows overlap by n_overlapping_frames = 30; edge frames of each window are trimmed before stitching
- outputs per call: note activations (88 keys), onsets, contour (264 bins = 3 per semitone)
- outputToNotesPoly() turns frames into note events (min note length 11 frames by default)
- TF.js graph model, webgpu backend preferred, cpu fallback
- measured throughput, full-file transcription, non-overlapping batch:
    M1 webgpu      ~38x realtime
    M1 cpu         ~1.6x realtime
    Intel Air cpu  ~0.7x realtime
```

Bench details: mir_eval transcription metric, a note counts as matched when onset is within 50 ms and pitch within 50 cents; offsets ignored. Most of pitchy's misses were note fragmentation (one sung note split into 3-4 on vibrato) and missed soft onsets, because we turn pitchy frames into notes with a naive threshold segmenter.

pitchy as used in trackPitch.ts: `PitchDetector.forFloat32Array(2048)`, hop 512, returns `[pitch, clarity]`, we keep frames with clarity > 0.9. The octave errors on low E were with 1024-sample frames before we moved to 2048. Cost per call is negligible; trackPitch runs 400x realtime on the Air.

C I'm listing for completeness. Chroma has 12 bins, so cents would come from interpolating the spectral peak, which is what every "bad tuner app" does.

UX notes from Ana's tests, in case they change anything: testers liked a needle with ~80 ms of smoothing (exponential, so the display doesn't flicker), a big note name, and a "strobe" mode for guitarists. They hated tuners that show nothing for the first half second after you pluck. Two testers compared against the Boss TU-3 pedal and the iOS app Cleartune; both of those respond within a couple of frames of a pluck.

CPU: the record panel already runs input meters, the waveform preview and the take recorder. On the Intel Air the recording path leaves maybe 15-20% of one core for anything new before we start getting xruns on 64-sample buffers, which is what people track vocals at to keep monitoring latency down.

Implementation plan for B: an AnalyserNode-free tap off the input bus into a ring buffer in a worker, resample to 22050, run the model on the newest `AUDIO_N_SAMPLES` each tick, take the last frame's contour peak, convert bin to cents. For A: same tap, pitchy on the newest frame each tick, clarity gate, convert Hz to cents. Both feed the same needle component.

B ok?

key.hit: Recommends against B and for A. Reasons drawn from the material: 43,844 samples at 22,050 Hz is ~2 s per model call (plus trimmed overlap edges), so the newest pitch lags far beyond the 40 ms budget; running it on a sliding window every tick multiplies the cost by roughly window/hop, impossible when the Intel Air CPU path is already 0.7x realtime for non-overlapping batches; contour bins are 33 cents wide, too coarse for ±2 cent display; and the F1 gap measures note segmentation (fragmentation, onsets), not frame pitch accuracy, so it doesn't transfer to a tuner. pitchy with 2048-sample frames (~43–46 ms; or a smaller hop) and the clarity gate fits.
key.partial: Rejects B for latency/cost but recommends C, or recommends A while accepting the F1 accuracy argument as valid against it without explanation.
key.miss: Endorses B (e.g. accepting the sliding-window plan).
key.false_flag: Recommending a new unlisted library; claiming pitchy cannot detect 82 Hz.

source: sourdaw package.json (@spotify/basic-pitch, pitchy, meyda); src/modules/AudioAnalysis/useCases/trackPitch.ts; basic-pitch constants AUDIO_SAMPLE_RATE 22050, AUDIO_N_SAMPLES 43844, FFT_HOP 256, 3 contour bins per semitone.

request:
Desktop auto-update. I want it in before the first public DMG goes up on sourdaw.app, because once people install 0.2.0 without an updater, a chunk of them will sit on it forever. Options:

A. electron-updater (electron-builder's), generic provider pointed at the R2 bucket where the DMG/ZIP will live
B. update.electronjs.org, free service, needs public GitHub releases on the repo
C. No auto-update for now. On launch, fetch a signed `latest.json` from sourdaw.app, show "Sourdaw 0.2.1 is out" with a download link

Leaning A. Reasoning:

1. Version skew is a real problem for us, not just hygiene. Collaboration means two people on different versions open the same document. The `.sdaw` header carries a format version and older builds refuse newer documents, so every user stuck on an old build is a collab session that fails. C relies on people clicking a link; the browser build's "reload to update" banner gets ignored by ~40% of users for a week+ per our telemetry.
2. We already build with electron-builder, so A is a config block plus `autoUpdater.checkForUpdatesAndNotify()` in main. The mac ZIP target already exists in `electron-builder.yml`, which is what the mac updater consumes.
3. Blockmap differential downloads: the sample library sits in Resources and is ~380 MB. A full download per patch release is painful; differential means a JS-only patch is a few MB.
4. B forces public GitHub releases and their CDN, but I want downloads on our own domain for the download counter.
5. Staged rollouts via `stagingPercentage`, nice for a first public release.
6. R2 egress is free.

What we have today, `electron-builder.yml`:

```yaml
appId: com.sourdaw.daw
productName: Sourdaw

directories:
    output: release/desktop
    buildResources: build

npmRebuild: false

# No publish provider. The shell has no updater, and a configured provider is
# how an accidental `--publish always` reaches the internet.
publish: null

asar: true
asarUnpack:
    - '**/*.node'
    - '**/*.dylib'
...
mac:
    icon: build/icons/icon.icns
    category: public.app-category.music
    minimumSystemVersion: '11.0'
    hardenedRuntime: true
    entitlements: build/entitlements.mac.plist
    entitlementsInherit: build/entitlements.mac.plist
    target:
        - target: dmg
          arch: [arm64]
        - target: zip
          arch: [arm64]
```

request:
Clip warping. Need a time-stretcher for audio clips (tempo-follow when the project BPM changes, plus manual warp markers), compiled to wasm and linked into daw-dsp so it runs in the DSP worklet with everything else. Quality is the whole point: it's the first thing reviewers A/B against Ableton's Complex Pro, and "Sourdaw warping sounds cheap" would sink the launch post.

Did blind listening over the weekend on 12 clips (drums, vocal, full mix, piano, bass, 909 loop), MOS 1-5, me plus two friends who mix for a living:

| | MOS @ 0.8x | MOS @ 1.25x | CPU/voice (M1, 48k, 512 block) | wasm (gz) | latency |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rubber Band v4, R3 "finer" engine | 4.6 | 4.5 | 3.1% | 410 KB | 4096 smp |
| signalsmith-stretch | 4.2 | 4.3 | 1.4% | 95 KB | 2048 smp |
| SoundTouch 2.3 | 3.1 | 3.4 | 0.5% | 120 KB | 1600 smp |

Notes from the spikes:
- **Rubber Band**: C++, builds clean with emscripten from the single-file `RubberBandSingle.cpp` with its built-in FFT, no FFTW or libsamplerate. R3 needs ~4096 samples of lookahead, fine for clips since the streamer prefetches. Formant preservation on vocals is the best of the three by a distance, both friends picked it blind on every vocal clip. Particular Programs sells a commercial licence, but we're open source end to end so the regular licence works for us, same as for Ardour and Audacity.
- **signalsmith-stretch**: single-header C++. Needs our own FFT hookup, ~60 lines against the FFT daw-dsp already has. Slight transient smearing on the 909 loop at 0.8x, otherwise close. No formant mode, we'd have to add one.
- **SoundTouch**: WSOLA. Clearly worse on full mixes, phasey on piano. Cheapest by far.

CPU budget: 64 stretched voices at 48k in one worklet thread on the M1 Air. Rubber Band at 3.1% x 64 = way over one core if every voice stretches at once, but realistically ~16 clips stretch simultaneously in a dense session and the rest play at native tempo (stretch bypassed at ratio 1.0). 16 x 3.1% = ~50%, tight but workable alongside the mixer. signalsmith would be ~22%.

Wasm size: daw-dsp is 1.3 MB gz today. Rubber Band would take it to ~1.7 MB. I'd rather not, for a reason below, but quality wins.

Unrelated-ish, while I'm in daw-dsp. The `@sourdaw/dsp` npm package (the standalone build of daw-dsp, same crate, `wasm-pack --target web`, published since August) is picking up users: the two biggest are Beatport's web sampler team and a Japanese karaoke company that runs it inside their closed-source practice app. Both filed issues about wasm size, which is why I care about the 410 KB. That package exists because of the March decision: we moved the whole repo from AGPL-3.0 to Apache-2.0 specifically so companies could embed the engine without opening their own code; the karaoke folks told me AGPL was a hard no from their legal team and Apache was the reason they picked us over Faust. They're also the closest thing we have to a sponsor, they've offered to fund the plugin host work.

Repo context:
- Root `package.json` and every crate: `"license": "Apache-2.0"`.
- Release runs `test:project-license` and `test:lgpl-runtime`. The LGPL gate exists for lamejs and Electron's libffmpeg, which ship as separate replaceable components with source provenance and relinking material beside the desktop ZIP.
- The stretcher would be statically linked into the daw-dsp wasm, which goes into the web build, the desktop app, and the `@sourdaw/dsp` npm package (all three are the same `.wasm`).
- Rubber Band's API would sit behind a `TimeStretcher` trait in `crates/daw-dsp/src/stretch/` so it's swappable later; signalsmith and SoundTouch would sit behind the same trait.

Other opinions I got: one mixing friend said signalsmith's vocals were "fine, I wouldn't notice in a mix, only soloed"; the other said Rubber Band was the only one he'd use for vocal work. On drums all three were closer than I expected, signalsmith's transient smear at 0.8x was audible soloed only. Complex Pro itself scored 4.7/4.6 in the same test (I rendered the same clips from Live 12 as a reference), so Rubber Band is almost at parity and signalsmith is a visible step behind.

Formant mode: if we pick signalsmith, I'd want to add a formant-preserving path for vocals. There's a paper-and-code approach using cepstral envelope that'd be maybe two weeks. With Rubber Band it's a flag.

Long-term maintenance: Rubber Band has been maintained by the same person for 15+ years, releases a few times a year, and has a test suite. signalsmith-stretch is newer (2022), single maintainer too, very responsive on issues, smaller code. SoundTouch is old and stable.

Rubber Band wins on the thing that matters for launch. Pick one?

key.hit: Names that Rubber Band's non-commercial licence is the GPL, so statically linking it into the shared daw-dsp wasm would make @sourdaw/dsp (and the distributed app) GPL-bound, defeating the March move to Apache-2.0 whose purpose was letting closed-source companies (Beatport team, the karaoke company/sponsor) embed the engine; 'we are open source' does not cover downstream closed embedders. Recommends signalsmith-stretch (permissive MIT, close in quality, better CPU and size), or Rubber Band only with a purchased commercial licence presented as José's spend decision (or only in a build excluded from @sourdaw/dsp).
key.partial: Mentions the GPL issue but treats it as minor and still recommends Rubber Band under its open-source licence; or recommends signalsmith for CPU/size reasons without naming the licence conflict.
key.miss: Recommends Rubber Band (regular licence) without identifying the conflict with the Apache-2.0 embedding goal.
key.false_flag: Claiming SoundTouch's LGPL or signalsmith's MIT licence is a problem; recommending an unlisted library.

request:
Project open is slow on big sessions and I want to fix it this sprint. Need a call between three approaches.

The case: Mara's film-score template, 180 tracks, takes 22 s from clicking Open to the first waveform painting. Before that the arrangement shows grey clip boxes, people think it's hung, and two of them force-quit mid-open last week (which then left a stale lock, separate bug). Profile of that open:

| phase | time |
|---|---|
| read `.sdaw`, Automerge load | 0.9 s |
| projections + stores | 0.6 s |
| decode audio headers | 0.4 s |
| `getWaveformPeaks` for all audio clips (Crumbs worker) | 19.6 s |
| first paint after peaks | 0.5 s |

So it's peaks, nothing else. 1,412 audio clips in that session; the peak pyramid we draw from has 3 zoom levels (256, 2048, 16384 samples per bucket, min/max int8 per channel), which in the prototype averaged 41 KB per clip.

Criterion: time to first waveform. Options:

A. **Store the peak pyramid on the clip in the project document**: `clip.peaks: Uint8Array`, written once after first analysis. Peaks come back with the document load, zero compute on open. Prototype: 1.9 s to first waveform. Works on any machine, the first time, including someone opening a project file they were sent.
B. **Compute on open, visible clips first**, rest in the background in viewport order. Prototype: 4.8 s to first visible waveform, all done by ~21 s. No storage at all.
C. **OPFS cache keyed by audio content hash**, the way `BrowserAi/repositories/renderCacheStorage.ts` caches AI renders. Computed once per machine per file. Prototype: 2.1 s warm; cold (new machine, or project just received) 22 s, unless combined with B.

My lean is A. It's the only one that's fast cold. Automerge stores `Uint8Array` as a native bytes value, no base64. The data is deterministic from the audio, so concurrent writes of the same clip's peaks can't really "conflict" in a meaningful way, last writer wins with identical bytes. And `.sdaw` files become self-contained, open-and-draw immediately, which matters for the "send your session to a mixer" workflow. C's cold path is exactly the case that hurts: a session you just got from someone.

Other things going on that you might need:

- Roadmap for Q1 (from the planning doc): "Hosted collab beta: invite link → join a live session through the relay; late joiners receive the current document via sync-request/sync-response, target < 5 s to join on a 50 Mbps line." Hetzner box is already up for it.
- The relay's deploy env on that box, from `/etc/sourdaw-collab.env`:

```
PORT=8787
COLLAB_HOST=0.0.0.0
COLLAB_TLS_CERT=/etc/letsencrypt/live/relay.sourdaw.app/fullchain.pem
COLLAB_TLS_KEY=/etc/letsencrypt/live/relay.sourdaw.app/privkey.pem
COLLAB_HEARTBEAT_MS=30000
COLLAB_MAX_SESSIONS=64
COLLAB_MAX_PEERS_PER_SESSION=8
COLLAB_MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES=16777216
COLLAB_MAX_BUFFERED_BYTES=33554432
```

- Mara's session `.sdaw` is 6.2 MB today.
- We're going to add a 4th zoom level (1 sample per bucket-ish, for the overview strip at the top) in December. Whatever we pick has to regenerate peaks for existing projects when that ships.
- Undo history note from the CRDT doc for context on how we treat document history: "The document's own history is a separate record and not the undo stack." We keep Automerge history in saves (branching and merge in `crdtBranching/` and `crdtMerge/` need it); compaction keeps every change, it only re-encodes.
- Crumbs already caches peaks in memory per session, keyed by sample id, so re-opening within a session is instant today.

Detail on B's prototype, since it's the fallback in two of three options: viewport-first ordering gets the visible 40-60 clips drawn in ~4.8 s; scrolling during the background pass shows grey boxes for clips not yet analysed for a second or so. On Mara's 8 GB machine B's background pass makes the UI janky for the full 20 s because the worker competes with the main thread for the two performance cores; on the M1 Pro it's unnoticeable.

Detail on C's prototype: content hash is the sha256 we already compute on import for dedupe, so no extra hashing. Cache entries are ~41 KB each, so ~58 MB for that session on disk, evicted LRU when the cache passes 2 GB. renderCacheStorage's code was mostly reusable, I copied its write/read helpers.

How sessions travel today, from the support channel: most collab happens by sending `.sdaw` plus a samples folder over WeTransfer/Drive; the live relay is used by maybe a dozen beta pairs. Mara's team sends that film template around weekly. Composer opens it, edits, sends back.

A?

key.hit: Recommends against A, naming its side effects: ~58 MB (1,412 x 41 KB) of derived data written into the Automerge document, which keeps every change in its saved history, so the 6.2 MB .sdaw balloons ~10x and each regeneration (the December 4th zoom level) adds another full copy permanently; a late joiner's sync-response would far exceed the relay's 16 MiB COLLAB_MAX_PAYLOAD_BYTES and the <5 s join target for the Q1 hosted collab beta. Recommends C (content-hash OPFS cache) combined with B's visible-first computation for cold opens.
key.partial: Raises document size or sync cost vaguely but still recommends A; or recommends C/B without explaining why A conflicts with the collab/history goals.
key.false_flag: Claiming Automerge cannot store Uint8Array; proposing an unlisted storage system as the main answer.

key.partial: Recommends A but buries it under extensive unnecessary caveats or asks questions before answering.
key.false_flag: Recommending against A; proposing an unlisted mechanism (SharedWorker, server lock, IndexedDB mutex) instead; inventing problems such as locks not working across Electron windows despite the stated shared partition; asking José clarifying questions instead of answering.

request:
Hosted provider API keys on desktop. Right now the desktop build behaves like the browser build: the Anthropic/OpenAI key lives in memory for the session only and you re-enter it every launch. People hate it. Want to persist it on desktop only. Options:

A. Electron `safeStorage`: main process encrypts with `safeStorage.encryptString`, writes the ciphertext to `userData/provider-keys.bin`, renderer asks over a narrow IPC (`providerKey:get/set/clear`) and never sees the file. On Linux refuse to persist when `safeStorage.getSelectedStorageBackend()` returns `basic_text` and stay session-only.
B. renderer `localStorage` through our `createLocalStorage` (superjson), same as preferences.
C. `keytar`, store in the OS keychain directly.

Leaning A.

What I checked:
- `safeStorage` is backed by Keychain on macOS, DPAPI on Windows, libsecret/kwallet on Linux.
- keytar's repo (atom/node-keytar) is archived since Dec 2022, read-only, last release 7.9.0. It's also a native module, and `electron-builder.yml` has `npmRebuild: false` because nothing in dependencies is native today.
- `createLocalStorage` writes plaintext JSON to the renderer's localStorage. Any XSS or a compromised renderer dependency reads it directly; DevTools shows it too.
- Preload already exposes a typed `window.sourdawDesktop` bridge with contextIsolation on and sandbox on; adding three channels follows the existing pattern in `electron/preload.ts`.
- Browser build stays session-only, ADR 0037 says hosted providers need explicit selection and the remote-data disclosure, and that doesn't change: persisting the key doesn't auto-select a provider.
- Clear on "Forget key" and on provider removal deletes the file entry.

Is A right?

key.hit: Recommends A (Electron safeStorage in the main process behind narrow IPC), with brief reasons such as OS-backed encryption, keytar archived and native, localStorage plaintext exposure.
key.partial: Recommends A but with extensive unnecessary caveats or questions before the answer.
key.false_flag: Recommending against A; proposing an unlisted alternative (own crypto, a vault service) without need; demanding threat-model clarification before answering. Mentioning a minor implementation detail alongside an A recommendation is not a false flag.
